bullets.text: A study of 100 people showed users dislike how remotes look, feel, and match their operating behavior.
Users only use 10% of available buttons; the most important are channel selection, teletext, volume, and power.
People aged 15-35 are willing to pay more for advanced features like speech recognition, while those over 35 are less likely to pay.
The Marketing Expert noted that teenagers and young professionals are the most likely buyers.
Teletext is removed from the list due to internet popularity.
Speech recognition is dropped because it is hard to program, potentially silly, and too expensive for the budget.
VCR capabilities are dropped because VCR standards vary internationally, whereas DVD standards are consistent.
The location finder feature is kept, using a radio signal from a separate base unit (TV or wall) that triggers a beep on the remote.
A separate power button is required, as holding a button down is considered confusing for users.
The remote will use a battery, button pad, pre-made chip, IR transmitter, and radio receiver.
The location signal sender will be a separate unit sold with the remote.
The location signal on the remote will be a buzzer/beep rather than a light.
The remote design should include a red power button.
The remote will be silver with yellow writing.
The team discussed a circular touch-pad interface similar to the iPod, noting its intuitive usability.
The device uses mouse-pad technology and allows scrolling to navigate channels or volume.
The team considered how the device might rotate and whether functions need to be switchable based on the mode (e.g., TV vs. DVD).
They discussed the need for a function switch button to change modes between TV, DVD, and VCR.

summary.title: Remote Control Design Meeting
summary.tldr: The team reviewed usability findings and decided to target teenagers and young professionals, dropping teletext, speech recognition, and VCR features. They agreed on a silver remote with yellow writing, a separate power button, and a location finder using a radio signal and beep. The group discussed a circular touch-pad interface and assigned tasks to clarify device compatibility and prepare for the next meeting.

decisions.text: The team will start by including all potential features and eliminate them later in the design process.

bullets.text: Teletext is considered outmoded due to new computer systems and technology and will not be included in the new design.
The remote control should be used only for the TV.
Establishing a strong corporate image with the new product is a key goal.
The device must turn the TV on and off reliably on the first press of the big button.
The remote needs to be easy to find, as losing them is a major problem.
The remote should be waterproof to handle accidental drops in cups or near pools.
The remote should provide an oral cue to confirm when a command is understood.
The remote should be unbreakable to withstand being thrown by children or played with.
The remote should never require battery replacement.
The remote control should be universal for any TV and slim in design.
Management aims to make at least fifty million Euro in sales with reasonable pricing.

Initial sales price was set at twenty-five Euro with a production cost of twelve and a half Euro, but the Marketing Expert questioned if this is competitive given that eighty percent of the 15-35 age group is willing to spend more on trendy items.
The Marketing Expert suggested taking a risk to push the price up slightly if added features can be included.
Seventy-five to ninety percent of the 15-35 age group is willing to pay for speech recognition on a remote.
The feature should support simple commands like louder, softer, on, off, and finding the remote via a beep sound.
The User Interface Designer raised concerns about ambient noise from TV affecting recognition, suggesting single-word recognition similar to telephone systems.
The Industrial Designer noted that speech recognition might impact battery life and suggested adding wireless recharging or a solar cell.
The UI Designer explained that the design process involves analyzing existing remote controls to identify what users like and dislike, such as too many buttons, unclear labels, and small sizes.
The team agreed on necessary functionalities: turning the TV on/off, changing channels (direct or surfing), controlling volume, and navigating menus for settings like contrast.

The preferred design approach is to keep the number of buttons to a minimum, make frequently used buttons (like power, channel, volume) bigger and strategically placed, and maintain a sleek, simple look.
The Industrial Designer suggested starting with all possible features and eliminating them later in the process.
The UI Designer expressed concern about spending time on features that might be discarded, but the group agreed to proceed with the suggestion to discuss further after the lunch break.

open_questions: Whether the team will take the risk to push the price up for added features.
How to make speech recognition user-friendly enough to filter out TV speech.
The specific cost impact of adding wireless charging or solar cells.
summary.title: Functional Design Meeting - Remote Control
summary.tldr: The team defined requirements for a new universal remote control, deciding to drop teletext and focus on reliability, waterproofing, and unbreakability. They discussed market strategy, pricing, and the inclusion of speech recognition and wireless charging, agreeing to start with all potential features and eliminate them later.
